Introduction and background Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a genetic blood disorder characterized by misshapen, crescent-shaped red blood cells and is associated with a range of complications that vary in both frequency and severity [ 1 , 2 ]. These complications, which include anemia, chronic pain, organ damage, and susceptibility to infections, significantly impact the lives of individuals with SCD [ 2 , 3 ]. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), an estimated 300,000 children are born with SCD each year, with about 75% of cases occurring in sub-Saharan Africa [ 4 ]. The Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study (GBD) indicates that between 2000 and 2021, the number of babies born with SCD globally increased by 13.7% (95% uncertainty interval: 11.1–16.5) to 515,000 (ranging from 425,000 to 614,000) births [ 5 ]. The WHO emphasizes that effective management strategies and preventive programs can potentially reduce the disease burden [ 5 ]. Andong (2017) reported that late diagnosis and chronic multisystem complications contributed to the low quality of life of patients living with SCD [ 2 ]. As a chronic illness with multiple comorbidities, SCD is recognized as both a non-communicable disease (NCD) and a significant contributor to NCD-related mortality [ 6 , 7 ]. Cardiovascular diseases, including heart disease, stroke, arterial and venous thrombosis, as well as chronic lung diseases such as pulmonary hypertension (PHT), kidney disease, and anemia, are among the leading causes of mortality in individuals with SCD. These conditions are also leading contributors to the global burden of NCDs, which in turn account for significant morbidity and premature deaths globally [ 8 ]. As the number of individuals living with SCD continues to increase, particularly in the Caribbean and sub-Saharan Africa, due to population growth and improved survival rates resulting from advancements in medical care, the burden of chronic diseases is also expected to increase [ 9 ]. Kanter and Kruse-Jarres (2013) reported that children and adults with SCD commonly experience comparable symptoms and challenges. However, with advancing age, the risk of chronic complications and disease progression increases, potentially contributing to early mortality [ 10 ]. These complications encompass a wide array of conditions, including avascular necrosis, sickle retinopathy, leg ulcers, pulmonary hypertension, nephropathy, thromboembolic complications, cardiac failure, transfusional iron overload, and decreased bone density [ 10 – 12 ]. The transformation of SCD from a severe life-threatening disease of childhood into a chronic, lifelong condition through the use of disease-modifying treatments imposes increasingly new challenges to healthcare providers and patients [ 13 ]. Among these challenges are physical, psychosocial, and emotional difficulties encountered by children with SCD. The need for chronic continuous treatments and regular multidisciplinary monitoring increases the social and emotional burden on patients and an increasing population of children with SCD who require long-term care [ 13 ]. This systematic review evaluates the burden and outcomes of chronic cardiovascular and pulmonary complications affecting adolescents (aged 10 to 19, as defined by the WHO) [ 14 ] and adults with SCD. Through a comprehensive search strategy and analysis of existing literature, we aimed to identify the prevalence and/or incidence of cardiovascular and pulmonary complications and demonstrate their impact on health outcomes among adolescents and adults with SCD. Mortality and low functional capacity rates arising from cardiovascular and pulmonary complications remain high in individuals with SCD [ 15 ]. Therefore, understanding the prevalence and clinical patterns of chronic cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in this population is crucial for guiding clinical practice and informing policy, facilitating the development of appropriate strategies and programs to alleviate disease burden and improve outcomes. Patients and methods Protocol registration This review was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), registration number CRD42023474623 (Additional file 1). Search strategy and eligibility criteria The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) served as a template for reporting the present review. The template is displayed in Additional file 2 [ 16 ]. Two reviewers (AN and NMK) developed a comprehensive literature search strategy. Major databases searched included MEDLINE/PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. No date or time restrictions were applied to the literature search. The search syntax for the PubMed database is provided in Additional file 3. This syntax combines MeSH subheadings and free-text keywords for the database search. AN searched for studies using keywords including sickle cell, burden, outcome, prevalence, incidence, and mortality. Additionally, chronic diseases were further delineated to include common cardiovascular and pulmonary complications, such as PHT, left ventricular diastolic dysfunction (LVDD), dysrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, myocardial infarction, venous thromboembolism (VTE), airway hyperreactivity, and sleep-disordered breathing. Boolean operators ‘AND’ and ‘OR’ were employed to incorporate search results for different concepts and synonyms within each concept. All identified articles were imported into the Rayyan software for further review [ 17 ]. The inclusion criteria for our study were as follows: i. Sickle cell disease patients (adolescents and adults). ii. Participants aged 10 years and above (adolescents 10–19 years, adults 20 + years). iii. Observational studies, including cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control designs. iv. Studies investigating cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in SCD. v. Availability of data on the prevalence and/or incidence of chronic cardiovascular or pulmonary complications. vi. Diagnosis of chronic diseases reported by standard methods. The exclusion criteria for this study were as follows: i. Literature reviews, systematic reviews, case reports, laboratory diagnostic tests, animal studies, autopsy reports, editorials and commentaries, conference abstracts, and clinical trials. Clinical trials and experimental studies were excluded to focus solely on observational studies, which best capture the real-world burden of the disease. ii. Unavailability of full-text article. iii. Lack of prevalence or incidence data. iv. Outcomes irrelevant to the scope of the study Eligible studies were included irrespective of language, year, or setting provided a full-text article was available in English. However, one Russian article was excluded due to the absence of a full-text English version for data extraction despite its abstract being published in English. Title and abstract screening were conducted independently by two authors (NMK and SMNB) using Rayyan [ 17 ], with any conflicts resolved by AN. All studies that met the inclusion criteria underwent full-text review by two reviewers (NMK and SMNB), with discrepancies resolved through consensus. Overall agreement between the reviewers ranged from 70 to 80%. The studies selected for inclusion in the narrative synthesis were imported into Zotero for reference management. Methodological quality assessment The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklist for cohort, cross-sectional, and case-control studies was utilized to assess the quality of included observational studies [ 18 ]. This checklist assesses 11 critical aspects for cohort studies, 8 for cross-sectional studies, and 10 for case-control studies. Two reviewers, NMK and SMNB, made the final decisions regarding study quality. Since there was no validation study to provide a cutoff score for rating study quality, a scoring system was devised for each tool. A well-conducted, high-quality study achieved scores of 11, 8, and 10 for cohort, cross-sectional, and case-control studies. Data extraction Data extraction was conducted in alignment with the study objectives and inclusion criteria. Relevant data was extracted concurrently by two reviewers, NMK and SMNB, using a standardized data extraction sheet in both Microsoft Excel and Word. The data extracted included the citation, study design, study location and setting, sample size, participant demographic information, chronic disease identified, outcome and measure of association, estimates of prevalence/incidence and associated factors, and other major findings. Specific data extracted included age and gender for demography and SCD subgroups such as hemoglobin (Hb) SS, HbSC disease, and sickle beta zero thalassemia (HbS β 0 -thal). Data analysis We performed a descriptive synthesis of all the studies included in the review, including synthesis of (a) PRISMA Flow, (b) a quality assessment using JBI tools, (c) a description of the study characteristics and findings, and (d) a narrative synthesis. Studies contributing to the Summary of Findings Table are detailed in Additional file 4, along with their references. Statistical analysis was conducted using R software version 4.4.1. The Microsoft Excel sheet containing data items was imported into R for analysis [ 19 ]. Studies were categorized into four groups: PHT, VTE, pulmonary diseases, and cardiac involvement (CI). Pooled prevalence for PHT, VTE, CI, and pulmonary disease was calculated by performing a meta-analysis of proportions using the DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model, allowing for more generalizable conclusions. Logit transformation was employed to transform the observed proportions and bring skewed data closer to a normal distribution. PHT, VTE, and CI prevalence were illustrated using a forest plot. Study heterogeneity was examined using the Cochrane Q test and quantified using I 2 values. Heterogeneity thresholds of 50% and 75% were used to indicate moderate and high levels, respectively [ 19 ]. The Baujat plot identified studies contributing to heterogeneity or outliers [ 20 ], while the leave-one-out analysis assessed each study’s influence on the overall summary proportion. A funnel plot and Egger’s regression test were used to assess for publication bias. A symmetry funnel plot suggested no publication bias, whereas an asymmetrical one indicated the presence of publication bias. If publication bias was confirmed, a trim-and-fill analysis was performed. Results Study selection The database search yielded 1174 records: 256 were obtained from PubMed, 504 from Web of Science, and 414 from Scopus. Additionally, one record was identified through a manual screening of citations. The studies yielded from the search were published between January 1, 1974, and October 12, 2023. A total of 541 duplicate records were removed, leaving 634 records for screening. After thoroughly screening titles and abstracts, we found that 517 records did not meet the criteria, and these were excluded. During this process, we identified one additional duplicate article, which may have been overlooked due to variations in some fields that the Rayyan software could not detect. Among 117 records identified for further review, 115 full articles were retrieved. Two articles were not retrieved and were excluded due to the unavailability of full text, despite efforts to retrieve them through database searches and direct communication with the authors, who did not respond. After assessing the full texts of the remaining 115 articles for eligibility, 36 were excluded. The 36 studies were excluded due to wrong study design, absence of relevant outcomes, wrong study populations, and age groups, small sample sizes, exclusive biomarker measurement (e.g., NT-proBNP), or potential bias from questionnaire-based assessments. We defined a “wrong study population” and “age group” as studies focused on chronic diseases in individuals with sickle cell trait or in children below age 10. Additionally, we categorized studies with fewer than 30 participants in each cohort as having a “small sample size.” Seventy-nine studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, of which 59 were eligible and included in the meta-analysis. The remaining 20 studies were excluded from the meta-analysis for various reasons, including reporting VTE in sickle cell trait with unspecified genotypes, unclear genotype subgroups, TRV measurement during an acute episode, use of large population datasets, and unrelated biomarker assessments. A summary of the study selection is presented within the PRISMA diagram (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Flow diagram showing the studies included Description of study characteristics The seventy-nine studies included observational studies conducted in the USA ( n = 43), Europe ( n = 14), Africa ( n = 11), the Middle East ( n = 4), the UK ( n = 3), Canada ( n = 1), and South America ( n = 1) and published between 2004 and 2023. Two studies ( n = 2) were conducted in both the USA and the UK. The majority of studies were observational cohort studies ( n = 52). Specifically, thirty studies were retrospective cohort studies, and twenty-two were prospective cohort studies. In Africa, most studies were conducted in Nigeria ( n = 10), which has the largest cohort of patients with sickle cell anemia worldwide [ 21 ]. Among the other observational studies, twenty-five were cross-sectional, and two case-control studies were retrospective and prospective (Fig. 2 ). Most of the studies ( n = 68) were conducted within hospital settings, while only eleven were population-based studies. The age range of participants across the studies spanned between 10 and 84 years. Fig. 2 Type of articles Subgroups: the subgroups identified in the studies included: (a) disease genotypes, specifically sickle cell anemia (HbSS), HbSC, hemoglobin SD disease (HbSD), HbS β 0 -thal, sickle beta plus thalassemia (HbS β + thal), (b) age-based groups; adolescents and adults, and (c) pregnant women. Several studies highlighted various confounding factors associated with cardiac and pulmonary diseases. For cardiac disease, notable confounders included hemolysis, lower fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels, valvular heart disease, dysrhythmia, Hb < 8 g/dL, and tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity (TRV) ≥ 2.5 m/s. Regarding pulmonary disease and PHT, confounding factors were age, gender, Hb, blood pressure, renal function, lactate dehydrogenase levels, blood urea nitrogen, lower HbF levels, and ferritin. Lastly, the confounding factors associated with VTE included age, elevated white cell count, length of hospital stay, and various other VTE risk factors such as the presence of central venous catheters, acute chest syndrome, osteonecrosis, vaso-occlusive crisis, stroke, severity of SCD (HbSS genotype), body mass index, history of thrombosis, hypertension, pregnancy, female gender, lower estimated glomerular filtration rate, and hydroxyurea use. Assessment of risk of bias All seventy-nine studies included in the review were independently evaluated for critical appraisal using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for cohort, cross-sectional, and case-control studies (Additional file 5). The results of this appraisal were used to generate a risk of bias rating for each study included (Table 1 ). Studies were classified as low risk with a score above 70% ( n = 74), moderate risk with a score of 50–69% ( n = 5), and high risk with a score less than 49% of bias ( n = 0). Among the 52 cohort studies, 5 were assessed as having a moderate risk of bias, while the remaining 47 were deemed to have a low risk of bias. All cross-sectional studies ( n = 25) and case-control studies ( n = 2) were appraised and categorized as having a low risk of bias. While right heart catheterization is considered the gold standard for diagnosing PHT, most studies did not perform this procedure. We postulated that this was due to the expense and unavailability of the procedure in many settings or anticipation of post-procedure SCD-adverse events. According to Maggio RD (2018), the rate of post-cardiac catheterization SCD-adverse events was reported to be 10% [ 22 ]. Therefore, noninvasive Doppler ECHO was recommended as the screening tool to suggest a diagnosis of PHT and establish risk categories based on peak TRV. In studies investigating VTE, including isolated deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE), the standard diagnostic tests used to confirm a suspected VTE included magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), compression ultrasonography for DVT or computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) for PE. Additionally, other pulmonary complications, including asthma and pulmonary dysfunction, were assessed using spirometry. Secondary outcome (meta-analysis) In most studies, mortality or increased risk of death was the main outcome associated with chronic diseases. However, not all studies included in the analysis reported specific outcomes related to the chronic diseases they investigated. In addition to mortality, reduced exercise capacity was a significant outcome of PHT. Studies evaluating VTE reported recurrent VTE, increased healthcare utilization and hospital stay, and maternal morbidity, among other outcomes. Additional cardiovascular and pulmonary outcomes noted included increased overall mortality, maternal mortality, and the development of cor pulmonale. Discussion This systematic review evaluated the prevalence of cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in adolescents and adults with SCD and their impact on health outcomes. Our review included 79 observational studies in narrative synthesis and 59 in quantitative analysis. Among the 79 studies, 74 were classified as low-risk for bias, while five were deemed moderate-risk. Because studies were characterized according to various chronic diseases and geographical regions, significant heterogeneity was observed in all estimates ( I 2 > 65%). This heterogeneity likely resulted from differences in clinical settings, sample characteristics, and outcome measures used. As a result, we employed a random effects model to obtain more conservative pooled estimates. PHT, VTE, and CI are common complications that affect patients with SCD [ 23 ]. The pathophysiology of cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in SCD is multifactorial. Intravascular hemolysis releases free hemoglobin, which depletes endothelial nitric oxide, a potent vasodilator, reducing its bioavailability and promoting vasculopathy and PHT [ 24 ]. Elevated soluble adhesion molecules (ICAM-1, VCAM-1, selectins) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (tissue necrosis factor, endothelin-1, interleukin-10) promote the adhesion of red blood cells, leucocytes, and platelets to the vascular endothelium, contributing to microvascular occlusion [ 25 ]. Activated platelets and endothelial tissue necrosis factor expression enhance the hypercoagulable stage [ 24 ]. In addition, ischemia–reperfusion injury, endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and oxidative stress contribute to myocardial injury through activation of both myocytes and non-myocytes [ 26 ]. Dysregulation of the renin–angiotensin system further exacerbates cardiac complications [ 24 ]. PHT was assessed using an elevated TRV measured by Doppler ECHO. ECHO remains the primary noninvasive screening tool for diagnosing PHT in SCD. However, its dependence on TRV and susceptibility to operator expertise, patient-related variability, and coexisting cardiac conditions limit its diagnostic accuracy, particularly in distinguishing pre- and post-capillary PHT. Because our prevalence estimates of PHT in adolescents and adults with SCD were based mainly on reported ECHO findings, variability in measurements can lead to under- and overdiagnosis of PHT. We recommend RHC to confirm PHT and standardized research protocols to reduce variability in assessing this patient population. The final pooled prevalence of PHT was 30% (95% CI 26–34), aligning with findings from previous observational studies on PHT in SCD [ 27 , 28 ]. Notably, Elfaki YA and colleagues recently reported a similar prevalence of 29% among a cohort of Sudanese patients with SCD [ 29 ], with even higher PHT rates documented by Klings ES and Fonseca GH [ 30 , 31 ]. According to a review by Ford and Gillard, the reported prevalence of PHT in adults with SCD ranges from 25 to 40% [ 32 ]. In adult patients, the prevalence of PHT is significant and increases the risk of death [ 27 , 33 ]. Additionally, PHT is associated with severe limitations in exercise capacity [ 34 ]. Studies evaluating PHT in children, including adolescents, reported a high incidence of PHT, although it was comparatively lower than that observed in adults. Sahoo et al. reported a PHT prevalence of 20.4% in children aged 5 to 14 years [ 35 ], similar to the 22.9% reported by Sokunbi et al. in children aged 5 to 18 years in Nigeria [ 36 ]. Comparably, a systematic review by Hariharan VS evaluating PHT among children and adolescents with SCA reported a prevalence of 22% [ 37 ]. In children receiving hydroxyurea, the prevalence of PHT was low [ 38 ]. Khargekar and colleagues demonstrated that a hydroxyurea dose above 20 mg/kg/day, with a mean rise in HbF of 18.46% post-hydroxyurea therapy, was beneficial in reducing TRV [ 39 ]. Klings ES et al. highlighted that in children ≥ 8 years, the TRV determined morbidity risk rather than mortality risk, providing a baseline for future comparisons [ 40 ]. In leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, excluding any individual studies did not substantially change the pooled prevalence of PHT, indicating robust findings. However, studies by Oni OO et al. [ 41 ], Musa BM et al. [ 42 ], and Mehari A et al. [ 43 ] produced the largest, although still modest, changes in the pooled estimate. These studies were influential primarily because they reported relatively extreme PHT prevalence estimates, were conducted in high-burden settings, and/or had smaller sample sizes, which increased their effect on both the pooled prevalence and the observed heterogeneity. We also employed a logistic regression model that included gender and region to examine sources of heterogeneity in reported PHT prevalence. The higher prevalence observed in high-income settings (the USA, the UK, parts of North Africa) may reflect greater diagnostic intensity, routine ECHO screening, and more standardized definitions of PHT. In contrast, lower estimates from West Africa likely reflect underdiagnosis, limited access to ECHO, survivorship bias, and shorter life expectancy in this setting. Furthermore, studies with a higher proportion of female participants generally reported lower PHT prevalence, suggesting a possible male predominance; however, this association did not reach statistical significance. Overall, substantial residual heterogeneity remained, indicating that other unmeasured factors, such as diagnostic criteria, disease severity, and healthcare access, likely contribute to the observed variability. VTE is a frequent complication of SCD. Several studies have highlighted the substantial prevalence of VTE in patients with SCD, with rates fluctuating between 8 and 25% [ 44 – 46 ]. In a longitudinal chart review of a cohort of patients, Lawrence and colleagues suggested that patients with VTE had greater SCD severity, evidenced by increased frequency of vaso-occlusive events and healthcare utilization [ 47 ]. Our study reported a pooled prevalence of 13% (95% CI 9–18), similar to the rate of 12.5% (95% CI 11.5–13.6) reported by Brunson and colleagues among patients with SCD by age 40 [ 46 ]. In the Cooperative Study of Sickle Cell Disease (CSSCD), the incidence of first VTE in patients aged ≥ 15 years was 11.3% (95% CI 8.3–15.3), with a higher risk of death reported among SCD patients with a history of VTE than those without [ 48 ]. It is worth noting that while the prevalence of VTE is reportedly high in this patient population, other studies have demonstrated low numbers of VTE events. Ajayi and colleagues reported a lower prevalence of 8.2% based on a medical record review of 783 individuals with SCD [ 45 ]. At an academic center in Saudi Arabia, VTE events complicated 3% of hospitalizations involving patients with SCD [ 49 ]. A substantially lower VTE prevalence of 2% was reported among adult patients with SCD in Nigeria [ 50 ]. Light J et al. investigated the impact of hormonal contraception (HC) on the risk of VTE in women with SCD. Among 219 women who used HC, 38 out of 184 (20.6%) experienced a VTE while actively using HC, whereas 20 out of 151 (13.2%) women who were never exposed to HC experienced a VTE. The study hypothesized that increased thrombotic risk was more likely influenced by disease severity than HC exposure [ 51 ]. In the leave-one-out sensitivity analysis for VTE, omitting either Okoye et al. (2022) [ 50 ] or Alkindi et al. (2021) [ 44 ] changed the pooled VTE prevalence. The influence of the two studies in the leave-one-out analysis likely reflects differences in study methods and patient populations. Okoye et al. examined a younger cohort with shorter follow-up and reported an unusually low VTE prevalence, while Alkindi et al. used a case-control design enriched for VTE cases, thereby increasing heterogeneity ( I 2 ). CI is a recognized complication in patients with SCD. The prevalence and types of cardiac manifestations vary based on the specific condition and population studied. While systolic heart dysfunction is relatively rare in SCD patients, diastolic dysfunction is more prevalent and serves as an indicator of severe disease and a high risk of mortality [ 52 ]. A study by Lopes et al. demonstrated that ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction were among the main cardiac alterations [ 53 ]. Our analysis yielded a CI prevalence of 24% (95% CI 17–33), which was notably high. An autopsy study of 306 patients revealed that CI was common, with cardiomegaly, myocardial micro-infarcts, and heart failure seen in 58%, 20%, and 10% of cases, respectively. Clinical manifestations were reported in 25% of patients, although autopsy findings suggested a high prevalence of 75%, raising concerns about an underestimated degree of CI [ 54 ]. Damy and colleagues evaluated ECHO abnormalities in adult patients with SCD. They reported a high prevalence of CI with left ventricular dilation in 35%, left atrium dilation in 78%, and cardiac output elevation in 23% [ 55 ]. However, at a single tertiary center for SCD in the UK, Natarajan and colleagues found that among patients who underwent a transthoracic ECHO, 17.5% had left atrium dilation, 11.3% had valvular heart disease, and 5.34% had left ventricular cavity dilation [ 56 ]. These values were lower than those reported by Damy and colleagues. The studies compiled herein showed a substantial frequency of cardiac abnormalities in patients with SCD. The development of a cardiac abnormality was closely associated with a pre-existing cardiac condition [ 52 , 57 ]. Bahashwan et al. reported a relationship between PHT and arrhythmias, highlighting that although arrhythmias are relatively uncommon in patients with SCD, they were observed in those at high risk of PHT. This finding emphasizes the importance of screening for arrhythmias in this patient subgroup, as early detection may help reduce mortality [ 58 ]. Given these findings, a CI prevalence of 24% in patients with SCD was within the range reported in previous studies, underscoring the importance of regular cardiovascular assessment in this population. Regular cardiovascular assessment can help detect and identify PHT and arrhythmias early, monitor left ventricular dysfunction, evaluate exercise capacity, prevent strokes, and inform treatment strategies. In our study, the most common cardiac and pulmonary complications were left heart disease, diastolic dysfunction, cardiac dilatation, heart failure, and PHT. Less frequent but clinically relevant complications included myocardial infarction, mitral valve regurgitation, coronary artery ectasia, non-rheumatic valvular heart disease, restrictive and obstructive lung disease, and PE. The prevalence of cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in SCD varies with age, sex, and disease severity. Pulmonary abnormalities may appear in early childhood but become more pronounced in adolescents and adults, who are at greater risk for chronic lung disease and PHT [ 59 ]. Although SCD has no predilection for either sex regarding its inheritance, studies suggest males are more vulnerable to complications, including skin ulcers, respiratory, musculoskeletal, and cardiovascular complications. Females more commonly experience anxiety and depression, as well as autoimmune conditions [ 60 , 61 ]. Individuals with severe genotypes, such as HbSS, are at the highest risk for these complications [ 62 ]. Risk factors and lifestyle aspects that contribute to the development or worsening of cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in SCD are closely linked to the underlying disease pathology. These factors include chronic hemolytic anemia, recurrent vaso-occlusive episodes, hypoxia, infections, and pre-existing chronic conditions [ 52 ]. Lifestyle and health-related factors, such as smoking, poor nutrition, dehydration, underuse of hydroxyurea, limited access to routine screening, and delayed diagnosis, play a significant role in exacerbating these complications [ 63 ]. Predictive indicators of cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in SCD include clinical symptoms and diagnostic test findings. Pulmonary complications often present with recurrent respiratory symptoms such as wheezing, exertional dyspnea, hypoxemia, exercise intolerance, and a personal history of asthma, allergies, or atopy [ 64 ]. Laboratory indicators include abnormal pulmonary function tests and elevated hemolysis markers such as LDH [ 65 ]. PHT may be suggested clinically by dyspnea on exertion and signs of heart failure, including elevated jugular venous pressure, a loud P2, and peripheral edema. Doppler ECHO, the 6-min walk test, and NT-proBNP are valuable in screening PHT in patients with SCD. Additionally, elevated serum creatinine, proteinuria, and chronic kidney disease are associated with increased cardiovascular risk [ 52 ]. More recently, biomarkers and imaging modalities such as serum ferritin, cardiac MRI with gadolinium enhancement, and T1 mapping are being incorporated into the assessment of sickle cell cardiomyopathy [ 66 ]. Current treatments help reduce the hemolytic and vaso-occlusive burden in SCD, but their direct impact on cardiovascular and pulmonary complications remains limited, particularly once organ damage has occurred. Hydroxyurea, a well-studied cytostatic agent, increases HbF levels and has demonstrated clinical benefit in reducing complications [ 67 ]. A 2024 meta-analysis showed that a daily dose of 20mg/kg significantly increased HbF and conferred protective effects when initiated early, helping to prevent cerebral, renal, and splenic injury [ 39 ]. Additional pharmacological treatments such as Voxelotor, Crizanlizumab, and L-glutamine offer complementary mechanisms by inhibiting hemoglobin polymerization, reducing vaso-occlusive episodes, and decreasing oxidative stress [ 9 ]. Significant global disparities hinder the management of cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in SCD. In low-resource settings, limited access to routine screening and inconsistent interpretation of findings delay timely diagnosis and intervention. While the NIH and American Society of Hematology guidelines advise against routine pulmonary function testing, screening is recommended as part of diagnostic evaluation when respiratory symptoms are present [ 68 ]. Similarly, the limited availability of ECHO, RHC, and longitudinal data impedes early detection of PHT and cardiomyopathy [ 64 ]. Access to advanced therapies, such as hydroxyurea, stem cell transplantation, and gene therapy, is limited by high cost [ 69 ]. Adjuvant options like chronic red cell exchange are frequently unavailable, and poor adherence to care and follow-up further delays diagnosis and long-term care, worsening outcomes in high-burden countries [ 70 ]. Reducing the burden of cardiovascular and pulmonary complications requires a comprehensive approach. Preventive measures include prophylactic antibiotics, vaccinations, regular health follow-ups, and lifestyle changes such as staying hydrated, managing exercise intensity, and avoiding extreme temperatures. Effective pain management and regular blood transfusions are crucial for managing SCD crises and preventing severe complications [ 71 ]. Our study has several limitations. The included studies varied in clinical settings, sample characteristics, and outcome measures, resulting in significant heterogeneity. This variability limited the analysis of outcomes and meaningful subgroup comparisons. Although meta-regression was conducted to explore sources of heterogeneity in PHT prevalence, analyses were limited to region and gender because of inconsistent reporting of age and genotype across studies. As with all study-level meta-regression, findings are subject to ecological bias, and residual heterogeneity remained substantial, limiting causal inference. In addition to limitations affecting prevalence estimates, a quantitative synthesis of morbidity and mortality data was not possible. Although some studies included reported associations using hazard ratios, risk ratios, or odds ratios, these estimates were based on heterogeneous outcome definitions, varying follow-up durations, and inconsistent adjustment of confounders. Furthermore, the attribution of mortality was uncertain, as some reported deaths may not have been directly related to the chronic complication under evaluation but to intercurrent factors, such as maternal mortality in severe SCD. Consequently, meaningful pooling of effect estimates was not possible, and morbidity and mortality outcomes were summarized narratively. The studies included in the review assessed the prevalence of chronic complications in adolescents and adults with SCD. However, most did not explicitly differentiate findings between the two groups, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions about age-related differences in prevalence. Notably, a study by Suell MN (2005) focused on patients aged 12 to 22.8 years reported a prevalence of PHT of 11% (9 of 80) among adolescents [ 72 ]. Additionally, the meta-analysis of VTE and CI complications included only eight studies for the pooled prevalence estimate, which may introduce bias. To address this, we performed sensitivity analyses, which included leave-one-out analysis, influential analysis, and Baujat plots, and assessed heterogeneity to minimize potential biases. Implications of findings Our study highlights a high prevalence and burden of cardiovascular and pulmonary complications, including PHT, VTE, and CI in adolescents and adults with SCD. The frequent overlap of these conditions, such as arrhythmias emerging in SCD patients with pre-existing cardiac disease or PHT, underscores the importance of prioritizing routine screening and proactive monitoring to mitigate progression, reduce hospitalization, and ultimately improve patient outcomes. Conclusion SCD is associated with a range of chronic cardiovascular and pulmonary complications that vary in severity and contribute to morbidity and mortality. Our meta-analysis reveals a significantly increased prevalence of specific cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in adolescents and adults living with SCD. Most studies in this review reported multiple outcomes or chronic conditions, emphasizing the need for careful monitoring to detect additional cardiac and pulmonary manifestations in individuals with pre-existing disease. We recommend routine screening and monitoring from age 5 to enable early detection and management of emerging cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in this at-risk population. Protocol amendments The following amendments were made to the initial protocol after registration on PROSPERO: The title was refined to specify the chronic diseases investigated: “Burden and outcomes of chronic cardiovascular and pulmonary complications in adolescents and adults with sickle cell disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.” The minimum age for adolescent participants was revised from 13 to 10 years, aligning with the WHO definition of adolescence. documents.title: Hematological Profile in Sickle Cell Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Comparing Steady-State and Vaso-Occlusive Crisis Phases (2000-2025).
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a genetic disorder characterized by intrinsic clinical manifestations, frequently exacerbated by vaso-occlusive episodes (VOEs), which significantly affect hematological parameters. This systematic review and meta-analysis is aimed at synthesizing evidence from studies published over the past 25 years on complete blood count profiles in SCD patients, both in the steady state and during VOEs. The objective was to clarify hypotheses and highlight the need for prospective studies to establish specific reference values for steady-state SCD patients, thereby improving patient management.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In accordance with the PRISMA guidelines and the Cochrane Handbook, a systematic search of major databases (including PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar) was conducted to identify analytical studies published between 2000 and 2025. Eligible studies compared complete blood count profiles in SCD patients during VOEs and in the steady state. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Extracted data were entered into Microsoft Excel 2013 and analyzed using R statistical software (Version 4.3.2). Between-study heterogeneity was evaluated using Higgins' inconsistency (Q) statistics, with results expressed as I2 values and corresponding p values. The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed using the ROBINS-E tool.
RESULTS: Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Pooled analyses demonstrated a significant impact of VOEs on hemogram parameters. This impact was characterized by anemia and erythrocytopenia (standardized mean difference [SMD], random-effects model: -0.97 [-1.45; -0.50]), accompanied by microcytosis (SMD, random-effects model: 0.18 [-0.21; 0.58]) and hypochromia (SMD, random-effects model: -0.90 [-2.96; 1.15]). These changes were also associated with reduced fetal hemoglobin levels, increased red cell distribution width (RDW), and reticulocytosis. Regarding the white blood cell lineage, VOEs were associated with leukocytosis (SMD, random-effects model: 0.73 [0.23; 1.24]) and a moderate increase across leukocyte subpopulations. Concerning the platelet lineage, VOEs exerted variable effects on platelet production, ranging from negative to positive influences, with an overall increase in platelet count (SMDs, random-effects model: -0.17 [-1.13; 0.78] and 0.78 [0.53; 1.03], respectively), accompanied by reductions in mean platelet volume and platelet distribution width (PDW).
CONCLUSION: This meta-analysis confirms the substantial influence of VOEs on red blood cell, white blood cell, and platelet parameters, as well as their associated indices. Importantly, although hematological parameters in the steady state are less severely altered than during VOEs, they often remain outside conventional reference ranges, reflecting a distinct physiological baseline in SCD patients. These findings underscore the urgent need for prospective studies to define specific hematological reference values for steady-state SCD patients, which is essential for optimizing their clinical management.

Introduction Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited hematological disorder characterized by the production of abnormal hemoglobin S, which deforms red blood cells (RBCs) into a sickle shape [ 1 , 2 ]. This morphological alteration increases RBC rigidity and impairs their passage through microvessels, leading to vaso‐occlusive episodes (VOEs), tissue damage, and chronic inflammation [ 3 ]. Globally, approximately 312,000 homozygous SCD births occur annually, with the vast majority (236,000) concentrated in sub‐Saharan Africa [ 4 , 5 ]. SCD thus represents a major global public health challenge, requiring coordinated and urgent management strategies [ 6 ]. Effective patient care demands a multifactorial and multidisciplinary approach that considers the various systems affected by the multiple complications to which SCD patients are predisposed [ 7 , 8 ]. Regardless of the system involved, the primary biological monitoring tool that provides an overview of the patient′s general condition is the complete blood count (CBC) [ 9 , 10 ]. The CBC allows for the evaluation of the quantity and quality of the three main blood lineages: RBCs (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leukocytes), and platelets [ 11 , 12 ]. This test is essential for diagnosing anemia, hematological malignancies, infections, acute hemorrhagic states, allergies, and immunodeficiencies [ 13 ]. Several factors considerably influence CBC results in SCD patients, with hemolytic and vaso‐occlusive crises being particularly significant [ 1 , 14 ]. Although infections, vaso‐occlusive events, and anemic crises are common in children with SCD, vaso‐occlusion has been reported as the most frequent manifestation and the leading cause of hospitalization, organ failure, and mortality in this population [ 15 ]. Vaso‐occlusion, which drives multiple pathogenic mechanisms responsible for numerous complications, is primarily caused by the adhesion of RBCs to the vascular endothelium, coupled with anemia, leukocyte activation, and platelet aggregation, resulting in elevated values that may predispose to complications [ 5 ]. The steady‐state period is defined as “a crisis‐free interval extending from at least three weeks after the last clinical event and 3 months or more after the last blood transfusion, up to at least 1 week before the onset of a new clinical event” [ 16 ]. Accurate interpretation of the hemogram in SCD patients remains challenging and requires reference values tailored not only to SCD patients in general but, more importantly, to those in the steady state [ 13 ]. Currently, interpretations often rely on standard WHO reference ranges [ 17 ]; however, steady‐state patients frequently display hematological values considered “abnormal” by these conventional standards, despite being clinically stable [ 11 ]. For example, Diallo et al. [ 18 ] reported a significantly lower mean platelet count during acute attacks (401.13 ± 138 G/L) compared with the intercritical phase (456.15 ± 164 G/L; p = 0.02), and a significantly higher prevalence of thrombocytosis during the intercritical phase ( p = 0.001) [ 18 ]. These observations highlight the need to establish a specific hematological profile for SCD patients in the steady state. In resource‐limited settings, where patient care and follow‐up are particularly challenging, defining such reference values is crucial for optimizing management and anticipating potential complications. This study is aimed at reviewing hemogram profiles reported in SCD patients over the past 25 years, both during VOEs and in stable conditions, in order to propose hypotheses and perspectives for prospective studies to define steady state–specific reference values. This approach could ultimately improve the management of SCD patients in Cameroon, across Africa, and globally. The clinical utility of this meta‐analysis lies in identifying objective biological signatures of VOEs. Consistent changes in CBC parameters between crisis and steady state may serve as a biological validation of acute episodes and support clinical decision‐making. 2. Methods This systematic review and meta‐analysis was conducted to assess the hemogram profile in sickle cell patients during both critical (VOEs) and steady‐state phases. Its primary objective is to inform the hypothesis and rationale for conducting prospective studies to establish specific hematological reference values for steady‐state SCD patients, aimed at enhancing their clinical management. 2.1. Search Strategy and Study Selection Articles were retrieved from the Google Scholar, Medline–PubMed, and Web of Science databases, selected for their rigorous indexing. The search strategy employed Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and combinations of keywords, including: “sickle cell disease AND blood count profile,” “blood count profile AND sickle cell disease in steady state,” “blood count profile AND sickle cell disease in steady state AND vaso‐occlusive crises,” and “sickle cell disease AND primary hemostasis.” Synonyms such as CBC and hemogram were also used. The search was limited to studies published between 2000 and 2025. Only studies that met the predefined objectives of this review were included. 2.2. Selection Criteria for Studies and Data Extraction Inclusion criteria encompassed analytical studies comparing haemogram profiles in SCD patients during both steady‐state and critical (VOEs) phases. Patients in the included studies were exclusively HbSS. Studies involving patients with different genotypes were not included. Two independent, qualified reviewers initially screened the titles and abstracts of all retrieved publications. Full texts of potentially relevant studies were then independently assessed against the inclusion criteria. Only studies indexed in English were considered. Studies meeting the initial screening were subjected to a peer‐review process before final inclusion. Any disagreements between reviewers were resolved by consensus. Data extraction was performed using a preformatted Microsoft Excel spreadsheet, with each variable clearly labeled at the top of each column to ensure structured and coordinated extraction. Extracted data were subsequently verified for accuracy and consistency. Information collected from each article included article identification details (DOI and journal name), study characteristics (authors, country, continent, year of publication, and study type), population characteristics (sample size, age, and sex), study methods (design, tools, and interventions), and main outcomes. 2.3. Outcome Measurement The CBC allows for the assessment of both the quantity and quality of the three blood lineages: erythrocytes (RBCs), leukocytes (white blood cells), and platelets [ 11 , 12 ]. Major factors such as vaso‐occlusive and anemic crises significantly influence this profile, and the final outcomes may vary depending on the presence or absence of a crisis [ 1 , 14 ]. The parameters used to define these outcomes in SCD patients were as follows: • Steady‐state period: Defined as the period free of crisis, extending from at least 3 weeks after the last clinical event and 3 months or more since the last blood transfusion, up to at least 1 week before the onset of a new clinical event [ 16 ]. • RBC line and erythrocyte parameters: RBCs (4–6 × 10 6 / μ L), hemoglobin (12–17 g/dL), hematocrit (HCT) (35%–55%), reticulocytes (50–120 G/ μ L), mean corpuscular volume (MCV) (80–100 fL), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) (27–29 pg), mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) (32–36 g/L), red cell distribution width (RDW) (11%–14%) [ 19 , 20 ]; • White blood cell line: Total leukocytes (4000–10,000/ μ L), lymphocytes (1000–4000/ μ L), monocytes (200–1000/ μ L), neutrophils (2000–7000/ μ L), eosinophils (50–500/ μ L), and basophils (0–100/ μ L) [ 19 ]. • Platelet line and parameters: Platelets (150–400 G/ μ L), mean platelet volume (MPV) (7–11 fL), platelet distribution width (PDW) (10%–17%), plateletcrit (PCT) (0.15%–0.35%) [ 20 ]. 2.4. Risk of Bias Assessment The risk of bias in the included studies was evaluated using ROBINS‐E, a tool designed to assess bias in nonrandomized studies of exposure effects [ 21 ]. ROBINS‐E examines seven domains of bias, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Each domain is assessed through a set of signaling questions intended to elicit relevant information about the study design and analytical approach. Most questions allow the response options “yes,” “probably yes,” “probably no,” “no,” and “no information.” Responses of “yes” and “probably yes” carry the same implications for risk of bias, as do “no” and “probably no” [ 21 ]. Figure 1 Flow diagram of the literature search. The domains evaluated included bias due to confounding, bias related to exposure measurement, bias in the selection of participants into the study or analysis, bias arising from postexposure interventions, bias due to missing data, bias related to outcome measurement, and bias in the selection of the reported result. All data were entered into a Microsoft Excel 2016 spreadsheet and analyzed using the aforementioned tool. 2.5. Data Synthesis, Management, and Analysis The statistical analyses were performed using R software, Version 4.3.2 (The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). All the included studies compared data between patients in VOEs and those in the steady‐state phase. Extracted data from the included articles were analyzed and presented as forest plots, comparing results from patients during VOEs with those in the steady‐state phase. Each outcome was accompanied by a narrative description. The mean difference and effect size between the experimental group (patients in VOEs) and the control group (patients in the steady‐state phase) were quantified using the standardized mean difference (SMD), as defined by Wan et al. (2014) in their study “ Estimating the Sample Mean and Standard Deviation From the Sample Size, Median, Range, and/or Interquartile Range ” [ 22 ]. Interpretation of SMD values was as follows: 0.2 ≤ SMD < 0.3: small effect, 0.3 ≤ SMD < 0.8: moderate effect, and SMD ≥ 0.8: large effect. Positive SMD values indicate an increase in the evaluated parameter in the experimental group, whereas negative values indicate a decrease [ 23 ]. Heterogeneity among individual studies was assessed using Higgins′ Q statistic, reported as I 2 with an associated p value [ 24 ]. Heterogeneity was classified as low: I 2 < 25 % , moderate: I 2 = 25 % –50 % , and high: I 2 > 50 % [ 24 ]. All analyses were performed with a 95% confidence interval, and p values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. 3. Results 3.1. Revision Process The initial search using specific keywords yielded 255 articles across the selected databases: 55 from Google Scholar, 135 from Medline–PubMed, and 65 from Web of Science. From this preliminary set, 47 articles were excluded because the full text was unavailable or the study objectives were not aligned with our review, leaving 208 articles for further assessment of study type and design. Subsequently, duplicates, review articles, perspective pieces, scientific reports, meta‐analyses, and descriptive studies were identified and removed. Ultimately, eight studies fulfilling the primary objectives of this review were retained for inclusion (Figure 2 ). Figure 2 Risk of bias assessment of nonrandomized studies of exposure effects using ROBINS‐E [ 21 ]. 3.2. Results of Risk of Bias Assessment Figure 2 presents the results of the risk of bias assessment conducted using the ROBINS‐E tool. Following the assessment, although some studies showed “some concerns,” the overall risk of bias across all included studies was generally rated as “low” (as illustrated in Figure 2 ). Heterogeneity was moderate, with an I 2 of approximately 60%, thereby supporting and justifying the presence of statistically significant differences between individuals with SCD (HbSS) and control subjects (HbAA). 3.3. Characteristics of the Included Studies The search period for the included studies spanned from 2000 to 2025. All selected studies were analytical case‐control studies, with the case group comprising sickle cell patients in the episodes (VOEs) phase and the control group comprising sickle cell patients in the steady‐state phase. The study populations included individuals of all ages and both sexes. Discussion SCD is a genetic disorder characterized by inherent clinical manifestations, which are markedly exacerbated by VOEs, thereby affecting hematological parameters. In contrast, the steady‐state phase is defined by the absence of VOEs, with milder clinical symptoms and generally less disrupted biological and hematological parameters [ 11 , 31 ]. However, interpreting these steady‐state parameters using conventional reference values from learned societies often categorizes them as “abnormal,” despite patients exhibiting clinical stability. This systematic review and meta‐analysis, covering studies from 2000 to 2025, aimed at synthesizing existing data on hemogram profiles in SCD patients. The fundamental clinical utility of this meta‐analysis lies in identifying objective biological signatures of VOEs. Currently, pain management relies on patient self‐assessment, which can be challenging in emergency settings [ 32 ]. Our findings are aimed at demonstrating that consistent changes in CBC parameters—specifically significant increases or decreases in certain values in patients during a crisis compared with their steady‐state phase—could serve as a “biological validation” of an acute episode. Standardizing these markers would not only help confirm VOE but also allow monitoring of the resolution kinetics to optimize the timing of hospital discharge. Analysis of the RBC lineage revealed that VOEs have a significant impact on its parameters. Specifically, our meta‐analysis demonstrated anemia and erythrocytopenia, with SMDs of −0.97 (−1.45; 0.50) and −1.11 (−1.83; −0.38), respectively, reflecting a substantial negative effect on hemoglobin levels. Conversely, VOEs were associated with a positive effect on reticulocyte production (SMD = 0.76 [0.46; 1.06]). These findings are consistent with the understanding that VOEs are strongly linked to RBC destruction and hemolysis, which are key contributors to SCD complications [ 33 ]. The progression of VOEs typically involves distinct phases: a prodromal phase (Phase 1) characterized by decreased RBC deformability and increased cell density, followed by hemoglobin reduction (Phase 2) [ 34 ], and culminating in biochemical and hematological changes, including anemia and reticulocytosis (Phase 3) [ 34 – 36 ]. Splenic sequestration, a major cause of acute anemia in SCD, further contributes to reticulocytosis by trapping RBCs in the spleen prior to atrophy [ 14 , 31 , 37 ]. Numerous studies corroborate these findings, reporting erythrocytopenia and anemia during the critical phase [ 38 , 39 ]. For example, Panigrahi et al. [ 27 ] in India observed significantly lower mean RBC counts (6.7 ± 2.15 T/L vs. 11.4 ± 4.4 T/L, p < 0.05) and hemoglobin levels (6.5 ± 2.27 g/dL vs. 11.39 ± 3.6 g/dL, p < 0.05) in patients experiencing crises compared with those in the steady‐state. Similar results have been reported by other researchers [ 10 , 28 – 30 , 40 – 42 ]. Moreover, the anemias observed are associated with an elevation of RDW, hypochromia, and reduced HbF. The SMDs reported using the random‐effects model were 0.68 (−0.24; 1.59) for RDW, reflecting a significant positive influence of vaso‐occlusive crises on RDW; −0.90 (2.96; 1.15) for MCH, and 0.01 (−1.40; 1.43) for HbF, reflecting a negative influence of VOEs on these parameters compared with controls. Indeed, Phase 2 of crisis development is often associated with an increase in the distribution width of RBCs and hemoglobin concentration [ 34 ]. RDW is a parameter that reflects the degree of heterogeneity in erythrocyte volume (anisocytosis) and is traditionally used in laboratory hematology for the differential diagnosis of anemias [ 43 ]. Its elevation in SCD indicates profound dysregulation of erythrocyte homeostasis, involving both impaired erythropoiesis and abnormal RBC survival. This dysregulation can result from a variety of underlying metabolic abnormalities, including telomere shortening, oxidative stress, inflammation, poor nutritional status, dyslipidemia, hypertension, erythrocyte fragmentation, and impaired erythropoietin function [ 44 – 46 ]. Hypochromia in SCD is associated with reduced serum ferritin and transferrin saturation levels, suggesting an imbalance between iron intake and the iron required for erythropoiesis. This imbalance leads to decreased hemoglobin levels in mature RBCs and reticulocytes, resulting in increased production of hypochromic erythrocytes and explaining the characteristic hypochromia observed in patients experiencing sickle cell crises [ 47 , 48 ]. In addition, the observed variations in MCV during VOEs warrant careful interpretation regarding hydroxyurea (HU) therapy. Although HU typically induces macrocytosis by increasing HbF levels, the relatively low baseline MCV in several included studies suggests a low prevalence of HU use in those specific cohorts, likely due to resource‐limited settings or coexisting iron deficiency. However, our meta‐analysis indicates a trend toward increased MCV during VOE, which could be an indirect marker of reticulocytosis and bone marrow stress. Future primary studies should systematically report HU dosage and adherence to better isolate the independent effect of VOE on erythrocyte indices [ 49 ]. Furthermore, the impact of HbF remains debatable, raising questions about the absence of a protective effect in sickle cell patients during crises. Although several hypotheses have been proposed, evidence suggests that VOEs may reduce HbF production in these patients, potentially contributing to more severe and painful episodes [ 50 ]. Interestingly, patients with elevated HbF levels may still experience severe disease. This phenomenon is attributed to the uneven distribution of HbF among F‐cells, whereas the overall average HbF remains unchanged. In such cases, the number of F‐cells may be insufficient to effectively inhibit HbS polymerization, despite elevated HbF levels [ 27 , 51 ]. Furthermore, regarding the white blood cell lineage, leukocytosis was observed along with a moderate increase in its subpopulations, with a SMD reported using the random‐effects model of 0.73 (0.23; 1.24), reflecting a significant positive influence of VOEs on white blood cell production. For neutrophils, the SMD was 0.37 (−0.63; 1.38). Indeed, in Phase 3 of VOEs, biochemical and hematological changes include leukocytosis [ 34 , 35 ]. Leukocytes, particularly neutrophils, play a critical role in the pathogenesis of VOEs. In mouse models of SCD, neutrophils have been identified as key contributors to microvascular obstruction [ 52 ]. Leukocytes are also central to the development of complications associated with SCD [ 53 , 54 ]. Clinical studies have demonstrated that leukocytosis correlates with disease severity and represents a risk factor for major SCD‐related complications, including stroke, acute chest syndrome, and early mortality [ 11 , 53 – 55 ]. For example, Panigrahi et al. [ 27 ], in India, reported a significant difference in white blood cell counts between sickle cell patients in crisis (15.1 ± 7.9 G/L) and those in the steady‐state phase (13.86 ± 8.82 G/L, p < 0.05). Similarly, Antwi‐Boasiako et al. [ 10 ], in Ghana, found higher white blood cell counts in patients during crises (14.5 ± 6.1 G/L) compared with those in the steady‐state phase (8.1 ± 2.2 G/L, p < 0.05). Comparable observations have also been reported by other researchers [ 29 , 30 ]. Regarding the platelet lineage, VOEs appear to exert a variable influence on platelet production, with an increase in platelet count (SMD = 0.78 [0.53; 1.03]) accompanied by a decrease in MPV (SMD = −0.40 [−1.14; 0.34]) and PDW (SMD = −0.09 [−0.35; 0.17]). PDW measures the variability in platelet size and is commonly used to differentiate platelet disorders, such as essential thrombocythemia from reactive thrombocytosis. Diallo et al. [ 18 ] and several other authors have reported significantly elevated platelet counts during the critical phase, associated with pronounced clinical manifestations in SCD [ 10 , 29 , 30 ]. Thrombocytosis, particularly when associated with increased PCT, may predispose patients to a hypercoagulable state, characterized by platelet activation and subsequent consumption. This process is markedly amplified during VOEs, with the release of E‐selectin, P‐selectin, soluble ICAM‐1, and tissue factor [ 57 – 59 ]. These changes are generally correlated with increases in MPV and PDW, although this differs somewhat from the observations in our findings. MPV is recognized as a marker of platelet activation and has been strongly associated with a higher frequency of VOEs [ 59 – 61 ]. PDW may therefore serve as a useful parameter to assess the severity of vaso‐occlusive crises in sickle cell patients. The main strength of this study lies in providing concrete, clinically relevant information regarding the impact of VOEs on each component of the blood count, thereby guiding patient management. Importantly, it highlights the need for prospective studies to establish a standardized database of hematological reference values specific to stable sickle cell patients. Limitations include the meta‐analytic nature of the study, which precludes methodological control over the included studies and may introduce selection bias. Additionally, the relatively small number of studies available limits the ability to fully support the proposed hypotheses for certain parameters. Another limitation of this study is that most of the included studies reported unadjusted data, without accounting for potential confounding factors such as age and sex. Nevertheless, the study provides valuable insights that can inform the management and treatment of sickle cell patients. 5. Conclusion SCD is a genetic disorder characterized by inherent clinical manifestations that are markedly exacerbated by VOEs, leading to significant alterations in hematological parameters. This systematic review and meta‐analysis synthesized studies published over the past 25 years to characterize these hematological profiles and explore their potential clinical utility. Our findings confirm the substantial impact of VOEs on all three blood cell lineages—RBCs, white blood cells, and platelets—as well as their associated indices. VOEs are consistently associated with anemia, erythrocytopenia, microcytosis, hypochromia, reduced HbF levels, elevated RDW, and reticulocytosis, alongside leukocytosis and variable platelet responses. Importantly, these recurrent and measurable changes suggest that hematological parameters could serve as objective biomarkers to support the diagnosis and monitoring of VOEs, complementing clinical assessment, particularly in settings where pain evaluation is challenging. In addition, although abnormalities are less pronounced in steady‐state patients, their values often remain outside conventional reference ranges, highlighting a distinct physiological baseline in this population. Consequently, this study underscores the need for prospective investigations to define standardized hematological reference values and validate their use as reliable tools for diagnosing VOEs and monitoring their progression and resolution, ultimately improving clinical decision‐making and patient care. documents.title: HLA Class II regulation of immune response in sickle cell disease patients: Susceptibility to red blood cell alloimmunization (systematic review and meta-analysis).
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Sickle cell disease (SCD) patients are commonly treated with red blood cell (RBC) transfusion. Pretransfusion tests commonly involve limited serological antibody testing. RBC alloimmunization to RBC antigens is a frequently encountered complication seen in chronically transfused patients. Genetic factors such as the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) are known to influence and regulate immune responses. HLAs are highly polymorphic and play an essential role in regulating immune responses, including RBC alloimmunization. The aim of this study was to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the association between HLA Class II allelic polymorphisms with the possible risk of developing RBC alloantibodies.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Four databases were systematically searched for relevant studies between the years 2000 and 2021 following the PRISMA guidelines. Four articles met the eligibility and quality criterion, and three alleles, HLA-DRB1*04, HLA-DRB1*15 and HLA-DQB1*03, that were found to be potentially associated with an increased risk in alloantibody formation were included.
RESULTS: The primary outcome measure was alloimmunization by RBC antigen exposure in multiply transfused SCD patients. The total estimate of alloimmunization of the SCD patients was 2.33 (95% CI, 1.58-3.44), demonstrating susceptibility to RBC alloantibody formation. Heterogeneity between the studies was insignificant, suggesting the differences associated with random sampling errors. The results showed that SCD patients carry an increased risk of producing RBC alloantibodies.
CONCLUSION: A strategy to prevent RBC alloimmunization is genotyping for genetically susceptible SCD patients receiving multiple transfusions. Early identification of genetic variants that can potentially increase the risk of RBC alloimmunization could aid in the screening process and selection of phenotypically matched RBC units.

Vox Sang . 2022 ; 117 : 1251 – 1261 . 36102140 10.1111/vox.13351 PMC9826043 Funding information None. Highlights HLA Class II alleles are associated with susceptibility to alloimmunization in multiply transfused patients with sickle cell disease (SCD). The variants HLA‐DRB1*04, ‐DRB1*15 and ‐DQB1*03 confer an increased risk of producing alloantibodies. Early identification of genetic factors affiliated with likely alloantibody development would allow selective use of phenotypically matched red blood cell units in genetically susceptible SCD patients. INTRODUCTION Background Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a hereditary condition affecting haemoglobin and blood flow within the body leading to pain and organ failure [ 1 ]. SCD is part of a wider group known as haemoglobinopathies and is most common in people of African ancestry. Transfusion of blood products is utilized as a supportive treatment of haemoglobinopathies to reduce morbidity and mortality [ 2 ]. Transfusion therapy can be highly beneficial to patients if the necessary safety precautions are considered. Unfortunately, the consequences of transfusions may still occur despite these precautions. SCD patients are highly susceptible to red blood cell (RBC) alloimmunization as they become reliant on blood transfusions (receiving multiple transfusions within their lifetime) to maintain a relatively healthy life. Among all transfused recipients, alloimmunization to RBC antigens usually occurs in about 2%–5% [ 3 ]. However, approximately 40%–50% of the transfused SCD patients develop RBC alloantibodies in the absence of RBC antigen phenotype matching beyond ABO and RhD matching [ 4 , 5 ]. Alloimmunization to RBC antigens in SCD patients has a significantly higher rate than other chronically transfused patient populations, potentially due to the differences in RBC antigen expression frequencies between people of different ethnic backgrounds (antigen disparity), high transfusion burden, genetic diversity and immune system considerations etc. [ 3 , 4 ]. As a result, RBC alloimmunization can complicate the selection of future compatible transfusion units and furthermore, increase the risk of haemolytic transfusion reactions (HTRs), and the development of additional RBC alloantibodies and autoantibodies in subsequent transfusions [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. Significance of RBC alloantibodies in polytransfused SCD patients The formation of alloantibodies and autoantibodies to RBC antigens has the potential to cause clinically significant complications that promote haemolysis, iron overload and RBC alloimmunization [ 2 , 9 ]. In SCD patients, the most common alloantibodies formed by multiple transfusions are anti‐C and anti‐E in the Rh blood group system and anti‐K from the Kell blood group system [ 2 ]. Therefore, SCD patients are usually transfused with ABO and RhD‐compatible, and phenotype matched with anti‐C, ‐E and ‐K negative RBCs as a preventative measure. Alloimmunization is less prevalent in populations where there is higher phenotypic compatibility between the donor and SCD recipient [ 10 , 11 , 12 ]. This is supported by the study conducted by Natukunda et al demonstrating a lower rate of RBC alloimmunisation in the Ugandan SCD population [ 12 ]. Role of HLA in alloimmunization Some studies have demonstrated that alloimmunized SCD patients show a worse survival rate than non‐alloimmunized patients [ 13 , 14 ]. It is not known why some patients become alloimmunized while others do not. This has raised questions about the contributions to the high rate of alloimmunization in SCD populations. However, it is known that the immune response is regulated by genetic factors such as human leukocyte antigen (HLA), having the ability to influence alloimmunization [ 5 , 14 , 15 ]. HLA genes are highly polymorphic and are involved in T‐cell‐mediated immunity [ 16 ]. HLA Class II molecules process and present RBC antigens by antigen‐presenting cells (APCs) to T‐cell receptors (TCR), which, in turn, activate CD4 helper T‐cells. This involves the interaction between T and B cells and the differentiation of B cells into plasma cells. CD4+ regulatory T‐cells (Tregs) are immune response modulators; the activation of T‐cells triggers Tregs to suppress the activation and proliferation of multiple cell types. A study has found that the Treg suppressive function is reduced in antibody responders in SCD patients [ 17 ]. Therefore, resulting in alloimmunization to RBC antigens. It is hypothesized that inheriting certain HLA alleles can predispose patients to RBC alloimmunization (Figure 1 ) [ 10 ]. FIGURE 1 Red cell alloimmunization in sickle cell disease patients after exposure to donor cells' antigens A relationship between HLA polymorphisms and immune responses to various RBC antigens has been established, and these include Duffy a [ 18 , 19 ], Kell [ 20 ], Diego [ 21 ] and Kidd a [ 22 ]. Noizait‐Pirenne et al conducted a study to identify the HLA‐DRB1 restriction molecules within the anti‐Fy a and anti‐K groups in Caucasians. Their study concluded that HLA‐DRB1*04 is the major restriction molecule for Fy a ‐derived peptides suggesting that stimulation can cause an individual to produce the antibody [ 18 ]. Similarly, Raos et al associated HLA‐DR and HLA‐DQ polymorphisms with alloimmunization to the Fy a antigen in a Croatian population [ 19 ]. Several studies have associated variants of HLA Class II with RBC alloimmunization and whether the inheritance of HLA Class II phenotypes provides susceptibility or protection against the formation of RBC alloantibodies [ 5 , 7 , 15 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ]. However, only a handful of these studies focused on the SCD population [ 5 , 7 , 15 , 23 , 24 ]. Many studies associated RBC alloimmunization with HLA‐DRB1 variants indicating the role of HLA restriction in susceptibility to forming RBC antibodies, particularly in multi‐responders. Maluskova et al demonstrated the association of HLA‐DRB1*15 with multiple antibody responsiveness in relation to Rh phenotypes [ 25 ]. This supported the hypothesis that certain HLA polymorphisms could further increase susceptibility to multi‐responsiveness towards RBC antigens. Scope of review Alloimmunization or the development of RBC alloantibodies is a major complication of blood transfusion, especially in chronically transfused SCD patients. Susceptibility to alloimmunization is dependent on several different factors, possibly leading to delayed HTRs (DHTR) or other adverse effects. However, not all patients exposed to mismatched RBC antigens become alloimmunized as only a minority of individuals form alloantibodies from exposure [ 27 ]. The differences in susceptibility have not yet been fully understood. As SCD patients, homozygous for the disease are multiply transfused, the exposure to different antigens increases the risk of alloimmunization. Some studies have associated HLA‐DRB1 with RBC alloimmunization risks. HLA Class II alleles could potentially be a risk factor for developing RBC alloimmunization upon exposure to foreign antigens. This study evaluates the presence of HLA Class II alleles in alloimmunized and non‐alloimmunized SCD individuals homozygous for the sickling phenotype. The primary aim of this study is to investigate the association between HLA phenotype and its correlation to RBC alloimmunization susceptibility within the multiply transfused SCD population. Second, to identify the HLA Class II alleles that can cause an individual with SCD to be more susceptible to forming RBC antibodies after transfusion. METHODS Study design A systematic review and meta‐analysis were conducted to investigate the association between HLA Class II polymorphisms resulting in alloimmunization. This study focused on the increased risk of susceptibility to RBC alloimmunization in SCD patients with HLA Class II genetic polymorphisms. Literature search strategy For identifying literature for the systematic review and meta‐analysis, the study followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐analysis) guidelines [ 28 ]. A systematic search on the PubMed, Scopus, Ovid and Google Scholar databases was conducted between the years 2000–2021, inclusive. The keywords (“HLA” OR “Human leukocyte antigen” OR “MHC”) AND (“Sickle cell disease” OR “Sickle cell anaemia” OR “SCD” OR “haemoglobinopathies”) AND “Alloimmunization” were used in conjunction during the searches. MeSH terms for variations in “HLA” and “sickle cell disease” were included to broaden the search. Furthermore, a manual search for additional literature was conducted. All articles retrieved underwent an eligibility criterion. Inclusion and exclusion criteria The PICO strategy (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) [ 29 ] was adopted for the study selection process to determine a generalized eligibility for inclusion of studies. Population: patients with SCD (homozygous for the HbSS genotype); Intervention: the HLA Class II allelic polymorphisms; Comparison: non‐alloimmunized individuals; Outcome: resulting in the alloimmunization of red blood cells (RBCs) confirmed by serological or molecular techniques. The criteria did not have a restriction on sample size or specific HLA Class II polymorphic gene. However, the inclusion criteria required (a) original articles, (b) the development of RBC alloimmunization associated with HLA polymorphism, and (c) a sample of patients with SCD (homozygous HbSS). Exclusion criteria were all articles that were (a) not in English, (b) duplicates, (c) other systemic reviews, (d) those unrelated to HLA or alloimmunization of RBCs or SCD, and (e) full texts that were unavailable. Data extraction The information obtained from the literature included the following information: author, year, sample size, objectives, design characteristic (prospective, retrospective), patient population, country of study implementation, HLA allele identified and methods used. Each study was assessed using a STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting Observational studies in Epidemiology) checklist [ 30 ] to investigate the suitability for the meta‐analysis. Statistical analysis Data collected from the studies compared the number of alloimmunized and non‐alloimmunized SCD patients with the presence of HLA‐DRB1*04, HLA‐DRB1*15 or HLA‐DQB1*03. The association between increased susceptibility to alloimmunization and HLA Class II polymorphisms was assessed using odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). From the selected studies, the binary random‐effect method utilizing the maximum likelihood model approach was selected to estimate the effect size as an odds ratio with 95% CI and heterogeneity. Significance was determined using p ‐value (where p ≤ 0.05 is considered statistically significant). The heterogeneity of the studies using the chi‐square‐based Q test and I 2 test relative to the degree of freedom was evaluated (where p ≤ 0.05 is considered statistically significant). Thresholds for the interpretation of heterogeneity follows: (i) 0%–40% might not be important, (ii) 30%–60% may represent moderate heterogeneity, (iii) 50%–90% may represent substantial heterogeneity, and (iv) 75%–100% considerable heterogeneity [ 31 ]. All statistical analyses were conducted using the Review Manager (RevMan) software (Version 5.4. The Cochrane Collaboration, 2020.) to evaluate the association between SCD patients and HLA alleles relative to RBC alloimmunization. RESULTS Study selection and characteristics of the included studies Between the years 2000 and 2021, a total of 866 articles were collected from the four databases, with an additional 17 articles manually found. Of these 883 articles, 850 articles were excluded, as described in Figure 2 . The remaining 33 articles were eligible for the systematic review. Among the 33 eligible articles, only four of these presented an analysis of HLA Class II alleles in SCD patients causing susceptibility towards alloimmunization and were included in the meta‐analysis.
